Now that I’ve left the hospitality industry, I’m trying to find ways to incorporate more movement into my day.
I have a day job, but it is based out of my house and it’s easy to get lazy about taking care of my health.
A lack of movement, even if I did fit in my allotted 30-60 minutes of moderate activity a day, would lead to me being sedentary for long periods of time, and therefore negating any of the benefits.
If you’re anything like me and work from home, I recommend setting up a small office.
I don’t mean one in the garage, or a desk in the living room or bedroom, I mean a small room with a computer, a phone, a printer, an air fryer, a microwave, and a kettle.
That’s just the way I do it anyway.
I find that even in my small space, if I walk a few laps around the room I can keep myself moving and break up the monotony of sitting all day.
Also, if the sun is shining I’ll sometimes open my windows for some fresh air.
What I find to be most effective however, is to pretend like I am actually leaving the house to go into work and create a commute!
I don’t own a car so that makes this a lot easier for me, but it could certainly apply to those who do drive.
I have the option to bike to work, but I find that in the winter it’s just too cold!
But, I get dressed into my work clothes as if I am leaving the house.
I eat breakfast before heading to work as well.
I head out and walk for 15-20 minutes.

I know it’s tempting to just go to meet people with the idea of raising money, I am guilty of that, and it can work, but you need to meet smart people in the space to actually learn what’s going on.

I met a few female founders which was fantastic (there needs to be more of us!) and met some people who had interesting businesses. I don’t want to just meet people to raise money, I want to be useful in the space.

As children, we generally go to school, do some sort of after school activities, and then come home and rest or do homework.
In high school, we might have a part-time job, so there’s a bit more to our daily life, but the general idea is the same.
In college, things get different.
Firstly, you don’t go to school every day; you go to school a few days a week for a couple of hours in the daytime.
The rest of the time you get to be free to do whatever you want, as long as you do your homework and get your degree.
After college, there are two general paths.
First, you can get a job at a corporation (I know, this may sound like it’s a lot to ask in this economic environment, but bare with me for a second).
A big corporation will likely put you into a position with very little job variation.
You’ll be sitting at a computer, doing pretty much the same thing, day after day.
So you’ve got the choice, do you want to make a boatload of money in a job that you hate, or do you want to have a good job that is enjoyable for you, and makes you happy?
## This is not a trick question.
If you said you wanted to make a lot of money and be very unhappy at your job, you’re a fool.
There is no excuse for that anymore, because there are now a ton of options for making a great living for yourself with an online business.
If you said you wanted to be happy at your job, then you’re just like every other person that has ever lived.
## But the question still remains: “how do I go about making my dream a reality?”
Well, I have some advice for you.

sentences.sentence: a blog I wondered about what the theme should be.
And I realized that I had been thinking a lot recently about what makes a life well-lived.
That got me thinking about the difference between living well and living morally.
It seemed to me that people often equate these two things and it seemed to me that they were often not at all the same thing.
And, perhaps most importantly, it seemed to me that living well was the point of living, and therefore, it made sense to organize my life around that, rather than morality.
Now at this point you might be thinking one of two things.
Either: a) this is a lot of pretentious, ivory-tower-dwelling nonsense, or b) that this is the sort of thing you’re meant to think about.
But if you’ve ever thought about it, you’ve probably thought, at least a little bit, about how one might live a better life.
And at that point, you might have started thinking about all the things you ought to do, if you were to live a better life.
And then you were probably overcome by guilt.
Or maybe you’re one of those people who think a life well-lived means never experiencing anything bad.
Or maybe you’re one of those people who thinks that a life well-lived must be a perfect replica of whatever that thing, whatever those things, are.
But even if you’ve never thought about this, you probably want to, in some way.
I certainly do.
This is where I think the problem begins.
I think that the problem begins when we think about how to live well, and we think about how to live well, morally.
And I’ll admit that I’m one of those people who sometimes think that in order to live a better life I need to live a more moral life.

sentences.sentence: learned these last six months.
I’m so grateful for all that I have:
– a healthy and comfortable house with my mom and two dogs
– two great jobs to build my own resume and develop my career path
– a community of women friends who are encouraging and inspiring
– a place where I can be creative
– a place where I can learn, grow, and be open to new things
– access to mountains and trails
– a healthy, whole, body that I can trust and rely on for every day hikes or a bike ride up Provo canyon
I’ve been learning, for the first time in my life, how to listen to my own body and my own mind.
I’ve been learning how to be gentle with myself and what my life should really be.
I’m learning that the only person who can bring me contentment is me.
It’s a long, hard road of self-reflection and listening, but it’s really helping me learn who I am and what I need to be happy.
I’m not learning to be selfish.
I’m learning to be aware.
I’m learning to really understand myself and accept myself for who I am.
I am learning that sometimes I can’t do it all, and that’s ok.
I’ve learned how to set limits, and boundaries, and it’s been so good.
I have never been happier.
I’ve found such comfort in simplicity.
There’s no one to judge me.
No one has an opinion on my life.
I’ve been able to create something great on my own.
I’ve been learning, and I’m so proud of it.
This is my journey.
No one else’s.

sentences.sentence: , daily schedule.
Wake up, walk a couple of miles, eat, write until 4 p.m. Eat, and watch Netflix until bedtime.
The first week was tough.
I wasn’t sure that I’d be able to follow the schedule, but I knew I could make it the first 15 minutes every day.
And so I did.
After the first two or three days, my fingers started hitting the keys with automaticity, my brain moving faster than ever before.
But then, something stopped me.
For the second or third time in a week, I heard a voice, “You’re going to be so disappointed when you realize you can’t do this.”
I put my head down and typed.
And typed.
The voice came back about every other hour.
At least three times per day, the voice came to me.
It wasn’t a negative voice, I didn’t want to stop or give up or anything, but it was the voice of doubt, the voice of reason.
The voice that said I wasn’t good enough for the conference, that the other writers were much better than me, and I would be a fool to go to this thing.
I should cancel it now, and let the money go to waste.
I didn’t stop writing, but I wondered why this voice kept coming back.
Every day for the first few weeks.
Then as the summer turned to fall, the voice became my constant companion.
My mind, always racing, began to be taken over by this voice.
It was all I thought about.
Every day, it got worse.
It told me I would fail.
Everyone would see.
My parents would be disappointed in me.
I was an impostor.
And when I got the manuscript into the hands of the literary agency to take a look at it, they would see it was garbage.

I put my head down and typed. And typed. The voice came back about every other hour. At least three times per day, the voice came to me. It wasn’t a negative voice, I didn’t want to stop or give up or anything, but it was the voice of doubt, the voice of reason. The voice that said I wasn’t good enough for the conference, that the other writers were much better than me, and I would be a fool to go to this thing. I should cancel it now, and let the money go to waste.

I didn’t stop writing, but I wondered why this voice kept coming back. Every day for the first few weeks. Then as the summer turned to fall, the voice became my constant companion. My mind, always racing, began to be taken over by this voice. It was all I thought about. Every day, it got worse. It told me I would fail. Everyone would see. My parents would be disappointed in me. I was an impostor. And when I got the manuscript into the hands of the literary agency to take a look at it, they would see it was garbage.
